query: For transition-metal catalysts, formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Shifting the d‐band center of the active metal sites in supported transition‐metal nanoparticles by a ligand/support modification is causally responsible for enhanced catalytic performance. In particular, moving the d‐band center approximately 0.3 eV downward (relative to the baseline) will weaken the adsorption of reaction intermediates, leading to improved activity and durability.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐synthesized supported transition‐metal nanoparticle catalysts (e.g., high‐entropy alloy catalysts or Pt‐based alloys) with an unmodified ligand/support environment and inherent d‐band center position.
generation.intervention: Apply a specific ligand or support modification (such as N‐doping or controlled ligand exchange) to tailor the electronic environment so that only the d‐band center is shifted, while keeping the particle size, morphology, and dispersion constant.
generation.conditions: Under typical catalytic reaction conditions (e.g., moderate temperature, controlled pressure, and appropriate reactant concentrations as in ORR or similar reactions) where the d‐band descriptor is predictive of adsorbate binding energies.
generation.structural_mediator: The d‐band center position of surface metal atoms, which mediates the interaction strength between the catalyst surface and reaction intermediates.
generation.mechanism: A downward shift in the d‐band center reduces the binding strength of key intermediates, optimizing their adsorption energies to lower reaction barriers while also mitigating deactivation processes such as particle growth or dissolution. This isolated electronic modification enhances catalytic kinetics and stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Catalysts modified to exhibit a ~0.3 eV downshift in the d‐band center will show measurably higher catalytic activity (e.g., higher current densities or turnover frequencies) and improved durability (less deactivation or particle agglomeration over time) compared to the unmodified baseline catalyst.
generation.baseline: A control catalyst prepared under identical conditions but without the ligand/support modification, retaining its original d‐band center position.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under moderate temperature and pressure conditions typical of the reaction of interest (e.g., the ORR in PEM fuel cell applications or analogous reactions), provided that other variables (such as particle size or morphology) are strictly controlled.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence supports a connection between d‐band center shifts and catalytic performance, the exact magnitude of performance improvement and potential secondary effects (e.g., subtle changes in particle stability or surface chemistry) remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one set with the tailored ligand/support modification designed to shift the d‐band center (modified catalyst) and one set without the modification (baseline catalyst). Ensure both sets have indistinguishable morphology, particle size, and dispersion. Test both sets under identical reaction conditions (e.g., in a rotating disk electrode setup for ORR or a similar catalytic measurement) to evaluate activity and durability.
measurements: Measurement of the d‐band center via XPS or ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) to confirm the shift in the modified catalyst.
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., current density, turnover frequency) to assess catalytic activity.
Durability tests (e.g., accelerated degradation or long-term stability tests) to determine catalyst lifetime under operating conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the catalyst with the engineered d‐band center does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >20% increase in activity or longer durability) over the baseline catalyst under identical conditions, or if the observed performance differences can be attributed to factors other than the d‐band center change, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

We calculated the partial density of states (PDOS) of Pt atoms at the (111) surface of N–Pt/HEA/C, Pt/HEA/C, and Pt foil. As seen in Figure S10, the d-band centers of N–Pt/HEA/C (111) and Pt/HEA/C (111) exhibit significant downshift relative to Pt (111), which is known to weaken the adsorption strength of intermediates on the surface Pt atoms and therefore accelerate the ORR process.− Notably, in comparison with Pt/HEA/C (111), the d-band center of N–Pt/HEA/C (111) showed a slight upshift trend, implying that N dopants can further regulate the interaction between surface Pt and reactants, thus optimizing the ORR performance, as discussed below.

To reveal the mechanism for the enhanced HOR performance over HEA SNWs/C, the surface properties of catalyst was studied by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurement. It is noted that all the metal elements in HEA SNWs are mixed with metal state and oxidation state. Compared to HEA NPs/C, the peak in the Pt0 4 f XPS spectrum of HEA SNWs/C positively shifts by 0.13 eV (Fig. 3a), while the peak in the Ru0 3p XPS spectrum negatively shifts by 0.36 eV (Fig. 3b), indicating that electrons might transfer from Pt to Ru in HEA SNWs. On the other hand, the Ni0 2p, Co0 2p, Fe0 2p and Mo4+ 3d XPS spectra of HEA SNWs positively shift by 0.26, 0.17, 0.93 and 0.25 eV, respectively, in comparison to HEA NPs (Supplementary Fig. 22). Considering that only Ru0 3p XPS spectrum negatively shifts by 0.36 eV, we might conclude that the positive shifts of Ni0 2p, Co0 2p, Fe0 2p, and Mo4+ 3d XPS spectra were attributed to the electron transfer from Ni, Co, Fe and Mo to Ru in HEA SNWs.
